issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette: Moana had always been a bright and ambitious young woman, with a promising career as an auditor ahead of her. But everything changed when she was stalked by a former acquaintance. The experience left her feeling constantly on edge, as if she was walking around with a target on her back. As the days turned into weeks, Moana began to withdraw from social interactions and situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. She stopped going out with friends, quit her book club, and even started avoiding family gatherings. When asked about it, she explained that she just didn't see the point of putting herself out there anymore - after all, what was the use when the world was such a dangerous place? Her loved ones tried to reassure her, but Moana had come to believe that her life had been irreparably destroyed by the trauma. The thought echoed in her mind like a mantra: "My life has been destroyed." Moana's work began to suffer as well. As an auditor, she was required to visit clients at their offices, but now she found herself hypervigilant whenever she stepped out of her own apartment. She would scan the streets for familiar faces, constantly checking over her shoulder, and wondering if she was being watched. Her colleagues noticed a change in her behavior and asked if everything was okay, but Moana just shrugged it off, saying she was "just being cautious". Deep down, however, she knew that this wasn't just about caution - she had to be on guard all the time because that's what the world demanded. As time passed, Moana started to internalize her negative appraisals. She began to tell herself that she deserved to suffer because of what happened - that somehow, she must have brought it upon herself. This self-punishing narrative played in the background of her mind like a perpetual hum, influencing every decision she made and every interaction she had. When faced with situations that might bring her joy or relief, Moana found herself avoiding them altogether. Why bother trying to feel better when the world was just going to hurt her again? Her loved ones grew increasingly worried about her, but Moana couldn't shake off the conviction that she was somehow broken beyond repair. Lately, things had come to a head. Moana's boss called her into his office, concerned about her performance and her increasing isolation from colleagues. He offered her support and resources, but Moana just felt overwhelmed by the thought of having to open up about her experiences again. It was then that she realized she needed professional help - not just to manage her symptoms, but to try and rebuild a sense of self-worth that had been shattered by the trauma. As she sat in his office, listening to his words of encouragement, Moana felt a glimmer of hope for the first time in months. Maybe, just maybe, she could learn to let go of some of that hypervigilance and start living again - but the thought was terrifying, because what if the world really was as dangerous as she believed it to be?
